title: Laravel 5 - How to access image uploaded in storage within View?
author: Stefan Bogdanescu

content: # Accessing Uploaded Images in Laravel Storage within Views When users upload avatars or other assets, you are often storing them in the `storage/app/public` directory via the `Storage::put` method or a file system helper. If your server configuration directs all web traffic to the `/public` root, you might find yourself stuck trying to serve files located in `storage/app/public` using a path like `/storage/uploads/avatar.jpg`. This results in a 403 Forbidden or 404 Not Found error because the web server does not know how to resolve that path directly. The core issue lies in the distinction between Laravel's internal storage facade and what your web server actually serves. The `storage/app/public` directory is designed to be accessible, but only if it is linked to a URL-accessible location. Without this link, the application code can read the file, but the browser cannot retrieve it via HTTP. ### Symlinking the Storage Directory The standard solution involves creating a symbolic link from `public/storage` to `storage/app/public`. This tells the web server that any request to `/storage/...` should actually resolve to the files in your application's storage directory. To implement this, navigate to your project root via terminal and run: ```bash php artisan storage:link ``` This command creates a symlink at `public/storage` pointing to `storage/app/public`. Once this link exists, you can access images using a simple URL path like `/storage/uploads/avatar.jpg`, assuming the file is placed in `storage/app/public/uploads`. With the symlink in place, your view can now render the image using the absolute path: ```html ``` This approach works because the URL `/storage/...` maps directly to the files on disk. However, relying solely on the symlink has a significant trade-off regarding security and deployment flexibility. ### Security Considerations with Symlinks While the `storage:link` command is convenient for development and standard deployments, it exposes the contents of your storage directory to the public internet. If you store sensitive data in `storage/app/public`, this method compromises that data immediately. Even though Laravel's storage facade provides methods like `Storage::disk('public')->get($path)`, which returns a file object, relying on symlinks for all assets makes it harder to restrict access to specific files without additional middleware or authentication checks at the web server level. Furthermore, symlinking can be problematic in containerized environments or when using certain hosting providers that do not support symbolic links out of the box. In those scenarios, manually copying the contents of `storage/app/public` to `public/storage` is a more reliable, albeit manual, alternative. ### Using Laravel's Storage Facade If you prefer not to rely on symlinks or if your application architecture changes frequently, you can serve files directly from within the view using Laravel's `Storage` facade. This approach abstracts away the physical file path and allows you to define a custom disk configuration in your `config/filesystems.php` file. You can configure a new disk that points specifically to the directory containing your images: ```php // config/filesystems.php 'public' => [ 'driver' => 'local', 'root' => storage_path('app/public'), 'url' => env('APP_URL').'/storage', 'visibility' => 'public', ], ``` With this configuration, you can retrieve the image URL directly within your Blade template: ```html ``` This method generates the full absolute URL based on your `APP_URL` environment variable. It is particularly useful when you need to switch between local and remote storage (like S3) without changing your view code. However, note that this requires the symlink to exist if you are using the default 'public' disk configuration in most versions of Laravel, or you must ensure the `url` path resolves correctly relative to your web root. ### Best Practices for Production In a production environment, always verify that the symlink exists before attempting to serve images. You can check this programmatically: ```php if (file_exists(public_path('storage'))) { // Safe to use public storage } ``` Additionally, ensure that your `.htaccess` file in the `public` directory is configured correctly to handle requests for non-existent files within the `storage` folder. If you are using PHP to serve images dynamically or if you need to apply access control, consider creating a dedicated route that serves the image content while checking user permissions before returning the response. By understanding how Laravel maps storage paths to URLs and configuring your environment correctly, you can ensure that uploaded avatars render reliably in your views without exposing unnecessary data or breaking your deployment pipeline.
